description: A minimal-size team with an idea for Lunar Landing Site Navigator solution.
summary:
PerfectSpot aims to make lunar site browsing easy and interactive.
See solar power and Earth visibility mapped on the Moon surface - for a selected date or a mission time span. Read them as colors and lines, calculated on-the-go based on NASA's lunar surface shape data. Apply different solar panels (such as static/rotary ones) and radio configurations (e.g. radio frequency influencing diffraction of waves) - observe the results chaning.
details:
PerfectSpot, as name suggests, helps find the perfect landing spot - on lunar south pole.

With the Sun and the Earth low over the horizon, this area is both an interesting mission target and a challenging one to assess: hills and crater rims decide whether a lander gets enough sunlight for its solar panels and a line of sight to the Earth for its radio. A small change in place or date can alter the answer. Open PerfectSpot in your browser to see a 3D globe of the Moon with a map of solar panel power and Earth visibility for a chosen moment or time span. Clicking any point (or entering its coordinates or a place name) shows a summary with a chart and basic data, including the next sunrise and sunset, Earthrise and Earthset. Map updates promptly when you change the dates, the panel's orientation (fixed, optimal, tracking the Sun or lying on the ground), the antenna mast height and the radio frequency (which affects diffraction of radio waves!). Everything is computed from NASA data: LOLA elevation models of the south pole on a 20 m grid, and the JPL DE440 ephemeris for the positions of the Sun, the Earth and the Moon. The globe shows Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter imagery, and automatic tests check the computations against JPL Horizons. Place names come from the IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature, and the landing sites of past missions from NASA NSSDCA records; both are shown on the globe.

The goal was to make complex data easy to explore. Easy means responsive: change a date or a setting, see the result on the map right away, and keep exploring. This turned out to be the key challenge. A map of a one-year time span may involve millions of sunrises, sunsets, Earthrises and Earthsets. Every point has its own horizon, found from the shape of the terrain around it. Computing this live with a naive method would be far too slow. We found the right algorithms and optimizations that have proven to do the job. The product is complex inside so that it can stay simple outside.

The frontend is a React and TypeScript single-page app built on CesiumJS. A GPU shader in browser draws the map layers, so colors and contour lines stay sharp at any zoom. The backend is written in Python with FastAPI, NumPy, Numba (compiled loops for the terrain scans), rasterio for the elevation data and SpiceyPy (NASA NAIF SPICE) for the ephemerides. A few of the backend's optimizations:

  • Each point's horizon is stored as a convex hull of the terrain in every direction, so a new date, panel angle or mast height needs no terrain re-scan.
  • Distant terrain is read from a pyramid of block maxima, which is coarser but never lowers a peak.
  • Shortcuts: only the directions the Sun and the Earth actually pass through in the selected time span are scanned. Times whose outcome is known without the horizon, such as the Sun being behind the panel, are skipped.
  • Caching: horizons are kept on disk in memory-mapped files that survive restarts, and an overview of the whole region is computed in advance after startup.
  • Online map best practices: the map arrives as tiles, coarse ones first, computed in parallel threads. Tiles the user has moved away from are cancelled.

The app created during the hackathon has proven to work, running both on a personal laptop and on a public cloud server. Of course, many improvements and extensions are possible; the most interesting are:

  • Cloud auto-scaling and rate limiting for public access
  • Support for other regions then the south pole (elevation models in other map projections in the backend)
  • "Find optimal location" button
  • Terrain slope as an additional limiting factor (rule out areas too steep for a lander)
  • Radio link power budget calculation
  • Data export as a downloadable report
